opus-5.5.text:
I think the really exciting thing is that the two approaches are complementary: they're good at almost exactly opposite things. Transformer-based models are remarkable at the fuzzy, creative, human-facing side of a problem. They can take an ambiguous natural-language request, propose a candidate program, guess a loop invariant, suggest a lemma, or translate an informal policy into something more structured. But they don't give you any guarantee that what they produced is correct. Constraint-based tools, SAT solvers, SMT solvers, theorem provers, model checkers, are the opposite. They're not creative in that sense, but when they tell you something is true, you can trust it, because it's backed by a proof grounded in mathematical logic.

So the pattern I see emerging, and that we're already building toward, is a kind of loop between the two. The language model proposes, and the reasoning engine checks. If the proof goes through, great, you have something with a real guarantee. If it fails, the solver often gives you a counterexample or tells you exactly where the reasoning broke down, and you can feed that back to the model so it can try again. That neurosymbolic loop gets you much further than either piece alone.

A concrete example is formalization. One of the hardest parts of applying automated reasoning has always been getting the specification right: what does the customer actually mean by "only people in my organization can access this data"? Language models can help bridge that gap, turning natural language into formal statements, while the logic tools can then check those statements for consistency, find ambiguities, and ask clarifying questions. You can also flip it around and use automated reasoning to check the outputs of generative AI, so answers about, say, an HR policy or a configuration are verified against a formal model of the rules, which helps catch hallucinations.

Proof search is another big area. Theorem proving has always involved a lot of human insight about which tactic to try or which intermediate lemma to introduce. Models trained on large corpora of proofs are getting quite good at suggesting those steps, and the proof checker keeps everyone honest. That could make formal verification dramatically cheaper and accessible to many more engineers.

So in the future I don't think it's one or the other. Generative AI will make it far easier to ask questions and generate candidate answers, and automated reasoning will provide the trust layer: the ability to say, with mathematical certainty, that this code, this policy, or this answer is actually correct. As AI systems take on more consequential tasks, that combination becomes really important.

r001.rationale: The response describes a general propose-and-check loop and gives several applications, but it does not clearly predict that the way the tools are combined will depend on the kind of problem being solved.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the most exciting things happening right now, and the way I like to frame it is that these two technologies have almost perfectly complementary strengths and weaknesses.

The transformer-based systems, the large language models, are incredibly good at the creative, intuitive part of the problem. If you give them a piece of code and ask "what's the invariant here?" or "what's the specification this function is probably supposed to satisfy?" they're surprisingly good at guessing. And guessing is a big part of what a human expert does when they do a proof. But the thing about those models is that they're not trustworthy. They hallucinate. They'll confidently tell you something is true when it's not. And in the domains I care about, security, correctness of systems that lots of people depend on, that's just unacceptable on its own.

Constraint-based tools, SAT solvers, SMT solvers, theorem provers, model checkers, they're the opposite. They're not creative at all. They can't come up with the lemma you need. But once you hand them a candidate, they'll tell you with mathematical certainty whether it holds or not. They don't get tired, they don't get fooled, and critically, when they say yes, you can produce a proof certificate that an independent checker can verify.

So the natural architecture is a loop. The neural model proposes, the symbolic tool disposes. The LLM says "I think this loop invariant is x is always less than n," the solver either confirms it or comes back with a counterexample, and that counterexample becomes feedback the model uses to try again. You're basically using the solver as an oracle that makes the model honest. And what's nice is that the whole thing is sound by construction, because nothing gets through unless the constraint solver signs off on it. The model's mistakes don't leak into your final result, they just cost you some compute.

We've been doing versions of this at AWS for a while now, long before it was fashionable, with the automated reasoning work behind things like IAM Access Analyzer and the Zelkova policy checker. The way the LLM pieces are coming in is they're dramatically lowering the barrier to entry. Historically, the hard part of formal methods was never the solving, it was writing the specification and getting the tool to do what you meant. Now you can describe your intent in natural language, let the model translate it to a formal spec, and then have the constraint tool check the actual system against it. And you can close the loop the other way too, use the formal tool to check the outputs of the model, so when a customer asks a question about their policy or their configuration, the answer that comes back isn't just plausible, it's actually been verified.

Where I think this goes longer term is that I expect the proof search itself to get a lot smarter. Right now solvers use heuristics that were hand-tuned by people over decades. There's a lot of room for learned guidance inside the solver, deciding which branch to explore, which lemma to try, where to spend your time. The distinction between "the neural part" and "the symbolic part" starts to blur, but the key property stays the same, the thing that ultimately decides truth is the piece you can check.

And honestly, I think that's the only responsible way to deploy this stuff at scale. If you want AI systems that act in the world, writing code, changing configurations, making decisions about access, you need something that can say no. The constraint solvers are that something. So I don't see them being replaced, I see them becoming more important than ever, because now there's a very fast, very prolific, very fallible author producing things that need to be checked.

r001.rationale: The response describes a general neural-proposal and symbolic-verification loop and gives security and correctness examples, but it does not say that how the tools are combined will depend on the kind of problem being solved.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re very complementary. Transformer-based systems are good at proposing things—programs, specifications, possible solutions—and constraint-based tools give us a way to check whether those proposals satisfy precise requirements.

Imagine a system that generates some code. We can ask a verification tool, “Does this code have the property we want?” If it doesn’t, the tool can produce a counterexample. That counterexample becomes feedback to the learning system, which can then try again. So you get this loop of proposing, checking, and refining.

The interesting challenge is expressing the right requirement. Proving that a program satisfies a specification doesn’t establish that the specification captures what you intended. I think there’s an opportunity for these models to help people articulate those requirements, too, with the constraint-based tools providing a rigorous foundation for checking the result.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re very complementary. Transformers are remarkably good at proposing things—whether that’s a program, an invariant, or a strategy for solving a problem. Constraint-based tools give you a way to check whether that proposal actually satisfies the requirements.

So you can imagine a loop where the model proposes a solution, a solver checks it, and, if it fails, produces a counterexample that helps the model try again. The model doesn’t have to be right on the first attempt, because we have an independent way of checking its work.

It goes the other way, too. There are lots of choices inside automated reasoning tools about what to explore next. Learning could help guide those choices while the underlying reasoning system maintains the correctness guarantees. That combination—flexible proposals with rigorous checking—is something I’m very excited about.
